analysis.one_liner: Restores pre-existing condition protections, but only if the Affordable Care Act is repealed first.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 83 Republican cosponsors but never received a committee markup or floor vote, and expired with the 116th Congress in January 2021 while the Affordable Care Act's protections stayed in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the health insurance rules only if Congress first passed a full repeal of the Affordable Care Act. In that scenario, it would ban insurers from denying coverage, charging higher premiums, or excluding benefits because of a pre-existing condition, and would guarantee that insurers must sell coverage to anyone who applies. It would also bar insurers from using genetic information for underwriting. It does not replace everything the Affordable Care Act does: it would not restore the law's premium subsidies, required essential health benefits, or Medicaid expansion.
analysis.who_benefits: If the Affordable Care Act were repealed and this bill became law, people with pre-existing conditions such as diabetes, cancer, or asthma would keep the right to buy insurance at the same price as healthy applicants, without benefit exclusions or denials for their medical history. Insurers would also gain in that scenario, because the repeal this bill is tied to would strip away the Affordable Care Act's coverage mandates and premium subsidies, while this bill re-imposes only a narrow slice of the consumer protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with pre-existing conditions, in a repeal scenario

how_it_helps.text: Bans private health insurance plans, in both the individual and group markets, from limiting or excluding benefits for pre-existing conditions.
Requires insurers to accept every employer and individual applicant who applies, with enrollment limited to open and special enrollment periods.
Prohibits setting eligibility rules or charging higher premiums based on health status, medical history, claims experience, disability, genetic information, or evidence of insurability.
Bars plans from collecting or purchasing genetic information for underwriting and from requesting or requiring genetic tests, with a narrow research exception.
Allows employer wellness programs tied to health-status standards to continue, subject to reward limits of up to 30 percent of coverage cost, rising to 50 percent if agencies approve.

analysis.who_pays: If it took effect, it would be alongside a full repeal of the Affordable Care Act, so the main cost would fall on the roughly tens of millions of people who rely on that law's premium subsidies, essential health benefits, and Medicaid expansion, none of which this bill replaces. Insurers would face guaranteed-issuance obligations without the individual mandate or subsidies that helped keep healthy customers in the market.
analysis.who_pays_short: ACA subsidy recipients and insurers, in a repeal scenario

drawbacks.text: Every provision takes effect only if Congress first enacts a full repeal of the Affordable Care Act; if no repeal passes, the bill has no force at all, tying a consumer protection to the removal of a larger set of protections.

The bill restores only the pre-existing condition, guaranteed-availability, and anti-discrimination rules; it does not restore the Affordable Care Act's premium subsidies, required essential health benefits, out-of-pocket limits, or Medicaid expansion, so coverage could remain guaranteed but unaffordable for sick and low-income people.

Guaranteed coverage for all applicants without the Affordable Care Act's mandate or subsidies raises the risk that healthy people stay out of the market and premiums for those who enroll, especially sicker people, rise sharply.

In the individual market, the bill omits the wellness-program safeguards that apply to group plans, and it explicitly permits employers' existing wellness programs to continue as long as current regulations remain in effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections on paper are real and would matter a great deal to anyone with a serious medical history, but they are designed to operate only inside a full repeal of the Affordable Care Act, which would remove far more support for ordinary people than this bill replaces. An honest reading is that the bill functions as a narrow backstop for one popular ACA protection while leaving the law's financing, benefit requirements, and subsidies behind, so in the repeal scenario it imagines, people with pre-existing conditions would keep access to coverage but would bear much more of its cost themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2019 and sent to three House committees, was referred to the Health Subcommittee a week later, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Greg Walden introduced the bill on January 18, 2019, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means Committees.
On January 25, 2019, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee of Energy and Commerce, where no further action is recorded.
83 House Republicans cosponsored the bill, but no Democratic cosponsors are listed.
The bill never advanced out of committee or received any vote in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
Because its provisions take effect only upon enactment of a full repeal of the Affordable Care Act, and no such repeal was enacted, the bill would have had no legal effect even had it passed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody moved the needle: the bill died quietly, the Affordable Care Act's existing protections stayed in force, and both patients and insurers kept the status quo under current law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; ACA protections remained in place

for.role: House Energy and Commerce Committee member and bill sponsor

against.name: Frank Pallone

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee and its Health Subcommittee.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 83 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic majority that controlled House committees and floor scheduling took no recorded action on the bill.

industries.note: If the bill took effect, insurers would have to guarantee coverage and charge sick people no more than healthy ones, but the repeal it is contingent on would also free them from the Affordable Care Act's coverage requirements and end the premium subsidies that bring them customers. Without a mandate or subsidies, guaranteed issue risks concentrating sicker, costlier customers in their risk pool.
